title: Manage Identity Lifecycle and Auditing
intro: Keeping AI identities governed over time: living inventories of human and non-human identities; provisioning and deprovisioning for joiners, movers, leavers and agents; periodic access reviews and continuous identity security posture management; and auditing AI resource use through token accounting, rate limits and session time-outs.
objectives: Build and maintain a living inventory of human and non-human AI identities, with owners, credentials, permissions and activity
Run provisioning and deprovisioning for people and agents that removes old access, revokes every credential type and transfers ownership
Design risk-based access reviews with usage context and automatic remediation, supported by continuous ISPM
Audit AI resource utilisation with per-identity token accounting, rate-limit and quota reviews, and risk-based session time-outs

blocks.title: You can’t secure identities you can’t see

scenes.title: You can’t secure identities you can’t see
scenes.sub: Inventories of human and non-human AI identities
scenes.say: Every review, revocation and investigation starts with the same question: which identities exist, and what can they do? | This video covers building and maintaining an inventory of human and non-human identities across AI systems.

scenes.title: What the inventory records
scenes.say: A useful inventory records six things about every identity. | Its identity and type: human, workload, agent or tool. | Its owner or sponsor: a named person who is still with the organisation. | Its purpose, and the systems and data it reaches. | Its credentials: what type they are, where they live, how old they are, and when they expire. | Its effective permissions: what it can actually do, which is often more than anyone intended. | And its risk tier, when it was last used, and when it was last reviewed.

scenes.title: Building a living inventory
scenes.say: A living inventory is fed automatically from several sources. The identity provider and HR systems supply people and their groups. | Cloud identity and access management supplies roles and service accounts. | AI platforms supply agents, API keys, model platform users and MCP server registrations, which traditional tools often miss. | All of this is correlated: duplicates merged, credentials linked to the identities that use them, and identities linked to owners. | The result is an identity inventory that stays current, with owners, risk ratings and activity, ready to drive reviews and incident response.

scenes.title: A static list and a living inventory
scenes.say: The difference between a static list and a living inventory is the difference between a record and a control. | A static list is updated by hand, perhaps each quarter. A living inventory updates continuously and automatically. | A static list covers what people remember to add. A living inventory is built from discovery across every platform. | So a static list is out of date as soon as it is written, while a living inventory can drive access reviews, alerts and incident response.

scenes.title: Risk signals in the inventory

items.d: Used by several people or systems

scenes.say: Once the inventory exists, it reveals risk. | Orphaned identities, with no current owner. | Dormant identities, unused for ninety days or more. | Over-privileged identities, holding rights they never use. | Long-lived secrets: old keys that have never been rotated. | Shared identities, used by several people or systems, which destroy accountability. | And external identities: third parties and partners whose access must end when their work does.

items: Record type, owner, purpose, credentials, permissions, activity
Feed it automatically from IdP, cloud IAM and AI platforms
A living inventory drives reviews, alerts and response
Watch for orphaned, dormant, over-privileged, shared and external
scenes.say: To recap. | For every identity, record its type, owner, purpose, credentials, effective permissions and activity. | Feed the inventory automatically from the identity provider, cloud IAM and AI platforms. | A living inventory, unlike a static list, can drive reviews, alerts and incident response. | And use it to find orphaned, dormant, over-privileged, shared and external identities.

blocks.md:
### Inventory fields
| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Identifier and type** | Human, workload, agent, tool or external service (Module 4.5) |
| **Owner or sponsor** | Accountability for purpose, permissions and retirement; must be a current employee |
| **Purpose and linked systems** | Links to the AI use-case inventory and AIBOM (Modules 2.1 and 2.5), so you know which models, data and agents depend on it |
| **Credentials** | Type (password, key, certificate, federated), storage location, creation date, expiry, rotation history |
| **Effective permissions** | The rights it actually holds, across direct, group and inherited assignments |
| **Risk tier** | Based on privilege, data sensitivity, autonomy and exposure |
| **Activity** | Last sign-in or use, typical volumes, last review date and outcome |
| **Lifecycle dates** | Created, last changed, planned end date for contractors, projects and temporary agents |

### Sources for AI environments
- **Identity provider and HR:** employees, contractors, groups and roles.
- **Cloud IAM:** roles, service accounts, managed identities, access keys; cloud infrastructure entitlement management (CIEM) tools calculate effective permissions.
- **AI platforms and gateways:** model platform users and roles, API keys per project, agent registrations, MCP server and tool registrations, agent cards for agent-to-agent connections (Module 4.1).
- **Secrets vaults and scanners:** where credentials live, and where they have leaked (Module 4.5).
- **SaaS management:** AI tools connected through OAuth grants, including those users approved themselves.

### Keeping it current
- **Discover continuously** rather than by survey; reconcile new identities against approved requests.
- **Require an owner at creation:** platforms should refuse to create service accounts, keys or agents without a named sponsor.
- **Expire by default:** temporary identities and agent credentials carry end dates.
- **Feed downstream processes:** access reviews (Section 3), deprovisioning (Section 2), detection rules and incident response all read from the inventory.

blocks.title: Name the risk signal
pairs: A service account whose creator left the company last year
Orphaned identity
An agent identity with no activity for four months
Dormant identity
A pipeline role with delete rights it has never used
Over-privileged identity
One API key used by three different applications
Shared identity
A consultant’s account with no end date
External access without expiry

blocks.title: Inventory questions
blocks.md: The inventory is the **foundation**: questions about reviews, deprovisioning or incident scope often have "establish a complete, owned inventory" as the best first step. Favour **automated discovery** and **mandatory ownership** over manual lists.

q.q: A CISO asks how many identities can reach the company’s AI training data. The IAM team can list employees, but not service accounts, API keys or agents. What should be done FIRST?
o: Send a survey to every team, asking them to list the service accounts and keys they use
Build an automated inventory from IdP, cloud IAM and AI platforms, with an owner for each
Revoke every non-human identity that can reach the training data, and wait for complaints
Report the employee count to the CISO, since people are the main risk to training data
q.why: Automated discovery across identity sources, with ownership, gives a complete, current answer and supports ongoing control. Surveys miss identities and go stale, mass revocation breaks services, and ignoring non-human identities misses most of the access.

sections.title: Provisioning and deprovisioning for AI identities

scenes.title: Joiners, movers, leavers, and agents
scenes.say: Access is easiest to get right at the moments when it changes: when someone joins, moves, or leaves, and when an agent is created, changed or retired. | This video covers provisioning and deprovisioning for human and non-human identities in AI systems.

scenes.title: Joiner, mover, leaver
scenes.say: For people, the HR system is the source of truth, and every change starts there. | A joiner receives birthright access to approved AI tools automatically, through the identity provider and SCIM, based on their role. | A mover gets the access for their new role, and, just as importantly, loses the access from the old one. Movers are where privileges quietly accumulate. | A leaver is disabled in the identity provider within hours, or immediately if the departure is hostile. | Then everything else is revoked: refresh tokens, OAuth grants to AI apps, personal API keys and active sessions. | Finally, ownership of anything they owned is transferred: agents, models, datasets and scheduled jobs.

scenes.title: The lifecycle of an agent identity
scenes.say: Agents need a lifecycle too. It starts with a request that states the agent’s purpose, its sponsor and its risk. | Approval covers exactly which tools and scopes it receives. | Provisioning creates its own identity and scoped credentials, and registers it in the inventory. | In operation, it is monitored, and its credentials are rotated automatically. | Any change to its tools or scopes goes back through approval, just like a new request. | And when it is no longer needed, it is retired: credentials revoked, tools removed, memory deleted and logs archived for the retention period.

scenes.title: Deprovisioning gaps in AI environments

items.d: Outlive the person who made them
Keep running after their owner leaves
Tools stay signed in for weeks
Datasets and fine-tunes with no owner

scenes.say: Disabling the main account isn’t enough in AI environments. Six gaps are common. | Personal API keys for model providers and AI platforms, which outlive the person who created them. | Agents built by the leaver, which keep running with no one responsible. | OAuth grants to AI apps, which hold refresh tokens that keep working after the password is gone. | Long-lived sessions in AI tools that stay signed in for weeks. | Scheduled notebooks and jobs that run under the leaver’s identity. | And datasets, fine-tuned models and prompts that no longer have an owner.

items: HR drives joiner, mover and leaver changes through the IdP and SCIM
Movers lose old access; leavers are disabled within hours
Revoke tokens, OAuth grants, keys and sessions; transfer ownership
Agents: request, approve, provision, operate, change, retire
scenes.say: To recap. | Drive joiner, mover and leaver changes from HR, through the identity provider and SCIM. | Make sure movers lose old access, and disable leavers within hours. | Revoke every token, OAuth grant, key and session, and transfer ownership of agents, models and data. | And give agents a full lifecycle: request, approve, provision, operate, change and retire.

blocks.md:
### Human lifecycle
- **Joiner:** HR creates the record; the IdP provisions **birthright roles** for approved AI tools through **SCIM**; additional access is requested and approved.
- **Mover:** access is recalculated for the new role; old access is removed, not just added to. Time-limited overlap may be allowed for handover.
- **Leaver:** disable in the IdP promptly (immediately for terminations for cause); revoke sessions, refresh tokens and OAuth grants; disable personal access tokens and API keys; reassign owned agents, models, datasets, notebooks and scheduled jobs; recover devices.
- **Contractors and partners:** accounts carry end dates; sponsors confirm continued need; federated partner accounts follow the partner’s own lifecycle (Module 4.5).

**Continuous access evaluation** standards (CAEP, part of the OpenID Shared Signals Framework) let an identity provider tell connected applications instantly that a session must end, rather than waiting for tokens to expire.

### Non-human and agent lifecycle
| Stage | Controls |
|---|---|
| **Request** | Purpose, sponsor, data and tools required, risk tier |
| **Approve** | Least-privilege scopes (Module 4.6); approval proportionate to risk |
| **Provision** | Distinct identity, short-lived or workload-based credentials, inventory entry, monitoring |
| **Operate** | Automatic credential rotation, usage monitoring, periodic review |
| **Change** | Any new tool, scope or data source goes through approval again |
| **Retire** | Revoke credentials and tokens, remove tool connections, delete memory and caches, archive logs per retention, update inventory and AIBOM |

Expire by default: temporary agents and project service accounts get end dates, and are disabled automatically unless renewed by their sponsor.

### Disable, then delete
Disable first: it is immediate and reversible. Delete later, once ownership of dependent assets has been transferred, investigations are closed and retention requirements are met. Deleting too quickly can break dependent services and destroy evidence; never deleting leaves dormant identities behind.

blocks.title: The departed data scientist
blocks.md: A data scientist leaves on good terms. IT disables her account the same day. Three weeks later, finance notices continued charges on a model provider account, and security finds that a scheduled notebook she wrote is still pulling customer data nightly, using a personal API key and an OAuth grant she approved for an AI analytics app.

q.q: Which improvement to the leaver process would MOST likely have prevented this?
o: Reminding departing staff in their exit interview to delete any keys and apps they created
Automatically revoking personal keys, OAuth grants and scheduled jobs, and transferring ownership
Disabling leavers’ accounts a full week before their last day, so there is time to check everything
Asking the model provider to block any further usage of the account once it notices leavers
q.why: Deprovisioning must cover every credential type and transfer ownership of running assets, ideally automatically from the inventory. Reminders rely on memory, early disabling doesn’t find hidden keys, and providers can’t know who has left.

blocks.title: Lifecycle questions
blocks.md: The best answers are **automated** and **driven by HR or the inventory**: SCIM for people, mandatory sponsors and expiry for non-human identities, and a leaver process that revokes **all** credential types and **transfers ownership**. Watch for movers keeping old access.

q.q: An ML engineer moved from the fraud team to the marketing team six months ago. A review finds she still has write access to the fraud model registry and fraud training data. What process failure does this show?
o: A joiner failure, because her original access was granted without enough checks
A mover failure: new access was added, but the old access was never removed
A leaver failure, because she should have been removed from the company directory
No failure, because engineers often help their former teams after moving
q.why: Mover processes must remove access that the new role doesn’t need. Accumulated privileges from past roles are a common source of excess access and toxic combinations.

sections.title: Access reviews and identity security posture management

scenes.title: Is this access still right?
scenes.sub: Periodic access reviews and identity security posture management
scenes.say: Access that was right last year may be wrong today. People change roles, projects end, and agents gain tools. | This video covers periodic access reviews, and identity security posture management, which checks identity risk continuously between reviews.

scenes.title: An access review cycle
scenes.say: An effective review cycle has six steps. First, scope it by risk: privileged access, sensitive training data, production models and agent permissions come first. | Collect effective access for every identity in scope, including service accounts, keys and agents, not just people. | The reviewer, ideally the owner who understands the access, decides to keep, change or revoke it, with context such as when it was last used and how it compares with peers. | Revocations are applied automatically, not left as tickets that stall. | Decisions are recorded as evidence for auditors. | And the process is measured: how much was revoked, how long reviews took, and what was overdue.

scenes.title: Rubber stamp or real review
scenes.say: Many access reviews are rubber stamps. Here is the difference. | A rubber-stamp review presents long lists of names and permissions. An effective review adds usage, risk and comparison with peers. | Rubber stamps go to whoever is assigned. Effective reviews go to someone who actually understands the access. | So rubber stamps approve everything, while effective reviews remove unused access and fix anomalies. | And instead of tickets that stall for weeks, effective reviews trigger automatic revocation.

scenes.title: Most granted permissions go unused
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative share of granted permissions used in the last 90 days
scenes.say: Usage data is the most powerful input to a review. In this illustrative chart, each identity type starts with the permissions it was granted. | But only a fraction are used within ninety days, and for service accounts and agents the gap is often largest, because permissions are granted generously at creation and never trimmed. | Removing unused permissions, starting with privileged and non-human identities, shrinks the attack surface without affecting anyone’s work.

scenes.title: What ISPM watches continuously
scenes.say: Identity security posture management, or ISPM, checks identity risk continuously, between periodic reviews. | It finds misconfigurations, such as accounts without MFA or weak identity provider settings. | Excess privilege: permissions that are unused or unusually risky. | Stale identities: orphaned and dormant accounts. | Risky secrets: old, exposed or shared keys. | Toxic combinations that break separation of duties. | And drift from approved baselines, such as an agent quietly granted a new scope.

items: Review by risk; include service accounts, keys and agents
Give reviewers usage and peer context; revoke automatically
Remove unused permissions, especially for non-human identities
ISPM watches misconfiguration, privilege, staleness, secrets, SoD, drift
scenes.say: To recap. | Scope reviews by risk, and include service accounts, keys and agents, not just people. | Give reviewers usage and peer context, and revoke automatically. | Remove unused permissions, especially for non-human identities. | And use ISPM to watch continuously for misconfiguration, excess privilege, stale identities, risky secrets, separation-of-duties conflicts and drift.

blocks.md:
### Periodic access reviews
| Review type | Typical frequency | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **Privileged access** | Quarterly or more often | Administrators of model platforms, registries, training clusters and identity systems |
| **Sensitive data and production AI** | Quarterly to semi-annually | Training data with personal data, production models, agent permissions |
| **Non-human identities** | At least semi-annually, plus event-driven | Service accounts, keys, agents, MCP servers: owner, need, scope, credential age |
| **General user access** | Semi-annually to annually | Access to AI tools and platforms |

Requirements vary by framework. For example, **PCI DSS v4.0** requires user accounts and access privileges to be reviewed at least every six months, and **ISO/IEC 27001** (Annex A 5.18) requires access rights to be reviewed regularly. **Event-driven micro-reviews**, triggered by a role change, a new scope for an agent or an anomaly, complement scheduled campaigns.

### Making reviews effective
- **Context:** last used, risk tier, peer comparison and recommendations (for example, "unused for 120 days: revoke").
- **Right reviewer:** the resource owner or sponsor, not just a line manager who can’t judge technical permissions.
- **Manageable volume:** pre-approve low-risk birthright access, and focus reviewer time on exceptions and high risk.
- **Closed loop:** revocations happen automatically, with exceptions time-limited and tracked.
- **Evidence:** decisions, reviewers and timing recorded for auditors.
- **AI assistance** can summarise usage and suggest decisions, but a person remains accountable for each decision.

### Identity security posture management (ISPM)
ISPM continuously assesses the security of identity infrastructure and identities: identity provider configuration, MFA coverage, privileged accounts, non-human identities, entitlements and secrets. It complements:
- **CIEM** (cloud infrastructure entitlement management): effective and unused cloud permissions.
- **ITDR** (identity threat detection and response): detecting attacks on identities in real time, such as token theft or abnormal sign-ins (Domain 5).
- **Secrets scanning** (Module 4.5) and **SaaS posture management** for OAuth grants to AI apps.

Typical ISPM findings drive remediation tickets or automatic fixes, and feed the next access review.

blocks.title: Review and posture vocabulary
cards: A periodic check by owners that each identity’s access is still needed and appropriate.
A small, event-triggered review, such as after a role change or a new agent scope.
Identity security posture management: continuous assessment of identity configuration, privilege and hygiene.
Cloud infrastructure entitlement management: calculates effective and unused cloud permissions.
Identity threat detection and response: spots and responds to attacks on identities in real time.

blocks.title: Review questions
blocks.md: Favour reviews that are **risk-based**, include **non-human identities**, give reviewers **usage context**, and end in **automatic remediation**. A review where managers approve 99% of access without information is a control failure, however well documented.

q.q: In a quarterly access review, managers approved 99.6% of 4,000 entitlements on the AI platform in under a minute each. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Require managers to sign a declaration that they reviewed every entitlement carefully
Add usage and risk context, route items to owners, and revoke unused access automatically
Double the frequency of the reviews to monthly, so problems are found sooner
Move the review to a spreadsheet, so managers can see all entitlements at once
q.why: Rubber-stamping comes from missing context and the wrong reviewers. Usage data, owner routing and automatic revocation make reviews meaningful. Declarations, more frequent rubber stamps and spreadsheets don’t fix the cause.

scenes.title: Following the tokens
scenes.sub: Token accounting, rate limits and session time-outs
scenes.say: Every AI request consumes tokens, compute and money, and each one is tied to an identity. Auditing that consumption reveals abuse, waste and compromise. | This video covers auditing AI resource utilisation: token accounting, rate limits and session time-outs.

scenes.title: Token accounting
scenes.say: Token accounting starts with every request, whether it comes from a person, an application or an agent. | An AI gateway meters it: input and output tokens, the model and version, latency and cost. | Each request is attributed to an identity, and through it to a team, an agent and a project. | Budgets and quotas turn that data into control, with alerts and hard caps. | Anomaly detection looks for spikes and new patterns against each identity’s baseline. | And reports provide showback to teams and evidence for auditors. None of this needs the content of prompts, so accounting can be done without storing sensitive text.

scenes.title: A leaked key shows up in the numbers
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative daily tokens for one application’s API key, in millions
scenes.say: Here is why per-identity accounting matters. In this illustrative chart, one application’s API key uses about three million tokens a day, week after week. | On day nine, usage jumps sixfold, then more than tenfold the next day, at hours the application is normally quiet. The key has leaked, and someone else is using it. | Because usage is attributed to each key and compared with its baseline, an alert fires, the key is revoked, and usage drops straight back. Without per-key accounting, this would only have shown up on the monthly invoice.

scenes.title: Session time-outs for AI tools

items.d: Sign in again after a set time

scenes.say: Sessions also need limits. | Idle time-outs, short for privileged consoles such as model platforms and training clusters. | Absolute session lifetimes, after which users must sign in again, however active they are. | Step-up authentication for sensitive actions, such as exporting data, approving agent actions or changing scopes. | Run-time limits for agents, so no task runs indefinitely. | Short-lived access tokens, with controlled refresh. | And revocation on risk: when signals change, such as a compromised device or a departure, sessions end everywhere at once.

scenes.title: What utilisation audits catch
scenes.say: Regular utilisation audits catch six kinds of problem. | Leaked credentials, which show up as new volumes, locations or hours of use. | Shadow usage: unapproved applications running on company accounts. | Runaway agents stuck in loops, burning tokens. | Model extraction, visible as high-volume, systematic querying. | Denial of wallet, where costs are driven up deliberately. | And plain waste: idle reserved capacity, or expensive models used where smaller ones would do.

items: Meter every request at the gateway and attribute it to an identity
Budgets, quotas and per-identity baselines turn data into control
Idle and absolute time-outs, step-up, agent run limits, revoke on risk
Audits catch leaks, shadow use, runaways, extraction, cost abuse, waste
scenes.say: To recap. | Meter every AI request at the gateway, and attribute it to an identity, team, agent and project. | Use budgets, quotas and per-identity baselines to turn usage data into control. | Apply idle and absolute session time-outs, step-up for sensitive actions, agent run limits, and revocation on risk. | And audit utilisation regularly to catch leaked credentials, shadow use, runaway agents, extraction, cost abuse and waste.

blocks.md:
### Token accounting
Record, per request: timestamp, identity (user, service, agent), application and project, model and version, input, output and cached tokens, latency, cost, rate-limit and policy decisions, and a correlation ID. **Prompt content isn’t needed** for accounting, so keep it out of accounting logs, or protect it as described in Module 3.5.

Uses:
- **Budgets and quotas** per identity, team and project, with alerts and hard caps (Module 3.6).
- **Baselines and anomaly detection:** sudden volume changes, new geographies, unusual hours, new models or endpoints.
- **Showback or chargeback:** costs visible to the teams that incur them, which also exposes unapproved use.
- **Evidence:** auditable records of who used which models, how much, and under which policies.

### Auditing rate limits and quotas
- Review configured limits against risk and actual need; remove "temporary" exemptions that became permanent.
- Track limit hits (HTTP 429 responses) by identity: frequent hits may mean abuse, a runaway agent or a limit that is too tight.
- Log every change to limits and quotas, with approver and reason.

### Session time-outs
- **Idle and absolute time-outs** proportionate to risk; for example, **PCI DSS v4.0** requires re-authentication after 15 minutes of inactivity for in-scope systems, and NIST SP 800-63B sets session limits that tighten with assurance level.
- **Step-up re-authentication** for sensitive operations (Module 4.5).
- **Agent sessions:** maximum run time, maximum steps and token expiry per task (Module 4.4).
- **Continuous access evaluation:** revoke sessions across applications when risk changes (Section 2).

### Making audits routine
Schedule monthly utilisation reviews for AI platforms, with exceptions investigated by the identity owner; send anomaly alerts to the SOC (Module 5.2); and keep accounting records for the period your policies and regulations require.

blocks.title: What does this usage pattern suggest?
pairs: A key’s token use jumps tenfold overnight, from a new country
Leaked credential
An agent makes the same tool call thousands of times in an hour
Runaway agent loop
One customer sends millions of systematically varied queries
Possible model extraction
Charges appear for an AI app nobody approved, on a company card
Shadow AI usage
Reserved GPUs sit at 3% utilisation for a month
Waste

blocks.title: Utilisation audit questions
blocks.md: Favour **per-identity attribution** at a gateway, **baselines with alerts**, and **budgets with caps**. A monthly invoice is not monitoring. For sessions, match time-outs to risk and add **step-up** for sensitive actions.

q.q: An organisation discovers a leaked model provider key only when the monthly invoice arrives at five times the usual amount. Which control would have detected it MOST quickly?
o: A quarterly review of model provider invoices by the finance team
Per-key usage attribution with baselines and real-time alerts on spikes
A policy requiring developers to report any key they think may have leaked
Reducing the number of models the organisation is allowed to use
q.why: Attributing usage to each key and alerting on deviations catches misuse within hours. Invoice reviews and self-reporting are slow or unreliable, and fewer models doesn’t detect anything.

quiz.q: Why must every non-human identity in the inventory have a named owner?
o: Owners are needed to calculate the licence cost of each identity provider seat
Someone must be accountable for its purpose, permissions and retirement
Identity providers refuse to authenticate identities that have no owner field
Owners receive copies of every prompt the identity sends to models
quiz.why: Without an accountable person, non-human identities drift, accumulate rights and are never retired.

quiz.q: Which source do traditional identity tools MOST often miss in AI environments?
o: Employee accounts created in the corporate identity provider
Agents, API keys and MCP server registrations on AI platforms
Group memberships synchronised from the HR system each night
Administrator accounts in the main cloud identity service
quiz.why: AI platforms create their own identities and credentials, which need to be discovered and correlated with the rest of the inventory.

o: An identity that belongs to an employee currently on annual leave
An identity that hasn’t been used for a long period, such as 90 days
An identity that can sign in only outside normal business hours
An identity whose password is due to expire within the next week
quiz.why: Dormant identities keep their access without being needed, which makes them attractive to attackers and candidates for removal.

quiz.q: Where do excess privileges MOST often accumulate in the identity lifecycle?
o: When new joiners receive their standard birthright access on day one
When people move roles, gaining new access without losing the old
When leavers are disabled in the identity provider
When contractors are given accounts with end dates
quiz.why: Mover processes that only add access leave people with rights from every role they have held.

quiz.q: Why isn’t disabling a leaver’s main account enough in AI environments?
o: Disabling accounts is reversible, so it doesn’t count as removal
Personal API keys, OAuth grants and scheduled jobs can keep working
AI tools ignore the identity provider once a user has signed in once
Regulators require all leaver accounts to be deleted on the same day
quiz.why: Keys, refresh tokens and jobs running under the leaver’s identity survive account disablement unless they are revoked too.

quiz.q: Why should an identity usually be disabled first and deleted later?
o: Deleted identities can never be audited, even while they still exist
Disabling is instant and reversible; deletion can break services or lose evidence
Disabled identities cost less to store in the identity provider than active or deleted ones do
Deletion requires approval from the regulator in most countries
quiz.why: Disable to stop access at once; delete once ownership is transferred, investigations are closed and retention is met.

quiz.q: What makes an access review effective rather than a rubber stamp?
o: Reviewers sign a declaration confirming that they checked every line
Usage and risk context, the right reviewer, and automatic revocation
Reviews are run more often, so each one covers fewer changes
All entitlements are exported into one spreadsheet for review
quiz.why: Reviewers need information and authority to judge access, and decisions must be applied without manual delay.

quiz.q: What does identity security posture management (ISPM) add to periodic reviews?
o: It replaces the need for any human decisions about access
Continuous checks for misconfiguration, excess privilege and stale identities
Real-time blocking of every single sign-in attempt that comes from an unfamiliar location
A single password for each user across every application
quiz.why: ISPM finds identity risk between review campaigns and feeds remediation and the next review.

quiz.q: Why do non-human identities often show the biggest gap between granted and used permissions?
o: Machines are given fewer permissions than people, so the gap is easier to see
Rights are granted generously at creation and rarely trimmed afterwards
Non-human identities can’t use more than one permission at a time
Identity providers hide which permissions machines actually use
quiz.why: Service accounts and agents are often created with broad rights "to make it work", and nobody revisits them.

quiz.q: What should token accounting record for each AI request?
o: The full prompt and response text, so that costs can be explained later
Identity, application, model, token counts, cost and policy decisions
Only the total monthly cost, as shown on the provider’s invoice
The user’s password hash, to prove who made the request
quiz.why: Attribution and usage data support budgets, anomaly detection and audit without storing sensitive prompt content.

quiz.q: A key’s daily token use jumps tenfold overnight, from a new country. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: A normal seasonal increase in customer demand for the product
A leaked credential being used by someone else
A billing error by the model provider that will be refunded
A successful upgrade to a faster model version
quiz.why: Sudden volume changes from new locations against a stable baseline are a classic sign of a stolen key.

quiz.q: Why should agents have maximum run times and step limits per task?
o: Long-running agents produce more accurate answers than short ones
They stop runaway loops consuming tokens, money and capacity
Model providers require agents to stop after a fixed number of steps
They let agents run without any rate limits on their tools
quiz.why: Run-time and step limits bound the cost and impact of agents that loop or go off course.

exam.q: After an incident, investigators can’t tell which systems a compromised AI agent could reach, because its permissions were granted ad hoc and never recorded. What should the organisation implement FIRST?
o: A policy requiring agents to log their own permissions in their system prompts
An automated identity inventory covering agents, with owners and effective permissions
A rule that all agents must be rebuilt from scratch every month to reset permissions
A quarterly survey asking teams which agents they run and what each can access
exam.why: A living inventory with effective permissions answers scope questions immediately and supports reviews and response. Self-reported prompts, monthly rebuilds and surveys are unreliable or disruptive.

exam.q: A contractor’s engagement ended two months ago. Her account was disabled, but an AI coding assistant she connected to the company’s code repositories through an OAuth grant is still pulling code nightly. What is the BEST process fix?
o: Ask contractors to disconnect any AI tools they connected before their last day
Revoke OAuth grants, tokens and keys automatically at deprovisioning, driven by the inventory
Ban all AI coding assistants for contractors, whatever the business need
Review the repository access logs once a year to find any AI tools that are still connected to it
exam.why: Deprovisioning must cover every credential type, including OAuth grants and refresh tokens, automatically. Relying on the leaver, blanket bans or annual log reviews leave the gap open.

exam.q: A team asks for a new autonomous agent with write access to the CRM and email. Which provisioning approach BEST fits identity lifecycle good practice?
o: Let the agent use the requesting team lead’s own account and mailbox, so that it can start work immediately
A request with purpose, sponsor and risk; approved scopes; its own identity, inventory entry and expiry
Create a generic service account with broad access, so future agents can reuse it
Provision the agent first, and complete the approval paperwork within the next quarter
exam.why: Agents need a governed lifecycle: a justified request, approved least-privilege scopes, a distinct identity, inventory registration and an end date. Borrowed human accounts and shared broad accounts break accountability and least privilege.

exam.q: An auditor finds that the AI platform’s access review covered only human users, and 1,800 service accounts and API keys were never reviewed. What is the BEST response?
o: Explain that service accounts are technical, so they fall outside the review’s scope
Extend reviews to non-human identities, with owners, usage data and automatic remediation
Delete every service account and API key that wasn’t reviewed, and recreate them as needed
Ask the platform team to confirm in writing that all service accounts are still needed
exam.why: Non-human identities often hold the broadest, least-used rights, so they must be in scope, reviewed by owners with usage context, and remediated automatically. Exclusion, mass deletion and written assurances don’t give real control.

exam.q: ISPM reports that 30% of identities with access to the model registry don’t have MFA enforced, including two administrator accounts. What should be done FIRST?
o: Schedule the issue for discussion at next year’s access review campaign
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on the two admin accounts now, then close the other gaps
Remove registry access from every identity, including the people who need it daily
Accept the risk, because the registry can only be reached from inside the corporate network anyway
exam.why: Privileged accounts without MFA are the most urgent exposure, so they are fixed first, followed by the rest. Waiting, blanket removal and accepting the risk on network grounds are all inappropriate.

exam.q: Finance asks for a way to control spending on AI services without blocking legitimate work, and security wants early warning of misuse. Which design BEST meets both needs?
o: A single shared API key for the whole company, with spending reviewed every quarter
Gateway metering per identity, with budgets, baselines and alerts, and caps per team
A ban on AI services until a full business case is approved for every use
Asking teams to estimate their monthly usage, and reconciling it against invoices
exam.why: Per-identity metering at a gateway supports budgets and caps for finance and baselines with alerts for security. Shared keys hide who used what, bans block legitimate work, and estimates don’t detect misuse.
